title: Teaching reading in Setswana foundation phase classrooms: How much phonics is too much?
text_snippet: Teaching reading in Setswana foundation phase classrooms: How much phonics is too much? Background: Teaching reading in African languages has been challenging in the South African context, given the poor performance of South African learners in international literacy assessments such as the Progress in International Reading Literacy Study PIRLS and, more recently, in the 2025 Funda Uphumelele National Survey (FUNS) by the Department of Basic Education. The continuous poor results are a serious call to action to address the reading crisis in South Africa. We argue that investigating teachers’ pedagogical practices can provide insights into how they teach initial reading in African languages. Objectives: Using the active view of reading as a theoretical lens, the study explores the preparedness of four foundation phase Setswana teachers to teach reading in Setswana in Gauteng. Method: The study employed a generic qualitative approach, with a case study design. The data were collected through semi-structured interviews and classroom observations with a sample of four Setswana foundation phase teachers. title: Investigating phonics instruction, meaning making, and heteroglossia within Grade 2 foundation phase isiXhosa classrooms
text_snippet: Investigating phonics instruction, meaning making, and heteroglossia within Grade 2 foundation phase isiXhosa classrooms Background: Early literacy teaching in South Africa has been shaped by policy reforms aimed at improving Foundation Phase reading outcomes. Although the revised national framework for teaching reading in African languages addressed longstanding curricular inconsistencies, concerns remain about its strong emphasis on phonics and the implications for reading for meaning in African language classrooms. Objectives: This study examined how a phonics-centred orientation shaped Grade 2 isiXhosa Home Language literacy practices and its implications for meaning making, learner creativity, and the use of learners’ multilingual resources. Method: A qualitative case study was conducted in two mother tongue-based multilingual primary schools in the Eastern Cape, South Africa. Data were generated through classroom observations, document analysis, and semi-structured interviews with three Grade 2 isiXhosa Home Language teachers. Data were analysed using a social practices perspective on literacy. Results: Literacy instruction strongly privileged phonics and code-breaking, with limited opportunities for sustained meaning making, learner creativity, and heteroglossic engagement. title: Where reading and writing begin: Foundational practices in Grade R and post-COVID-19 implications for teacher education
text_snippet: Where reading and writing begin: Foundational practices in Grade R and post-COVID-19 implications for teacher education Background: Early reading and writing readiness begin before Grade 1. In Grade R, cognitive and motor skills support learners’ ability to listen, remember, follow instructions, recognise symbols, and engage in early writing activities. Objectives: This study examined Grade R learners’ cognitive and motor skill development and considered their implications for early reading and writing readiness. Method: A quantitative expost facto research design was used. Data were collected from Grade R learners and teachers using a Cognitive Development Scale or Test, a Motor Skills Development Scale, and a teacher questionnaire. The data were analysed using descriptive statistics. Results: Learners were rated above average in overall cognitive and motor skills development. Cognitive skills such as memory, remembering details of a just-read story, following instructions, and alphabet recitation supported early literacy readiness. Motor skills such as tracing, drawing, name printing, letter spacing, and number spacing supported early writing readiness. title: Identifying morphological errors in the English of Deaf learners in Lesotho
text_snippet: Identifying morphological errors in the English of Deaf learners in Lesotho Background: Morphological awareness (MA) is widely recognised as contributing to successful reading and reading comprehension. Despite this, research examining the nature of morphological errors among second-language (L2) English learners remains limited, particularly among Deaf learners. Objectives: This study identified and classified English MA errors made by Deaf learners in Lesotho and determined the most prevalent error types and their possible underlying sources. Method: Data were collected from 26 Deaf learners in Grade 3 to Grade 7 at a school for Deaf learners in Lesotho. Learners completed five MA tasks assessing inflectional and derivational morphology. A taxonomy was developed to identify and classify the morphological errors. Results: Overall performance on the MA tasks was low, providing important context for the high frequency of errors. Learners achieved a mean score of 15% for inflectional awareness and 26% for derivational awareness. The analysis identified intralingual errors, including overgeneralisation and the incomplete application of English morphological rules. title: Knowledge and practice standards for pre-service language and literacy teachers: Looking back, looking forward
text_snippet: Knowledge and practice standards for pre-service language and literacy teachers: Looking back, looking forward Background: In 2016, the South African Department of Higher Education and Training initiated a project to develop standards to guide English and Mathematics teacher educators in curriculum design and implementation. Objectives: The investigation aimed to identify key affordances and limitations of the Primary Teacher Education (PrimTEd) knowledge and practice standards for the teaching of English, and to identify directions for their refinement and take-up. The article traces the conceptual foundations of the draft standards, examines their alignment with current language and literacies education scholarship, with South African directions in language education, and with conceptions of teacher knowledge. It also explores how the standards are being interpreted in teacher educator practice. Method: Using the frame of reflection-on-action, reflection-in-action, and reflection-for-action, the study makes use of documentary sources and vignettes to provide a literature and practice-informed account of the standards. It draws on archival material, recent scholarship in the field of language and literacies teaching and learning, South African education policy documents, and accounts of la

title: Folklore-based pedagogy for literacy and critical thinking in Sepedi classrooms
text_snippet: Folklore-based pedagogy for literacy and critical thinking in Sepedi classrooms Background: South African primary schools continue to face significant literacy challenges, with PIRLS 2016 finding that 78% of Grade 4 learners were unable to read for meaning. In Sepedi-speaking communities, the gap between indigenous oral traditions and formal education deepens these challenges, as culturally significant folklore resources remain underutilised. Objectives: This study examined the pedagogical potential of Sepedi folklore including folktales (dinonwane), proverbs (diema), and riddles (dithai) as culturally responsive tools for developing literacy and critical thinking among Grade 7 Sepedi home language learners in the Lebowakgomo Circuit, Limpopo. Method: A qualitative design used semi-structured teacher interviews, non-participant classroom observations and document analysis of learners’ folklore-based activities. Participants were purposively selected, and data were analysed thematically using inductive coding. Results: Sepedi folklore functioned as an effective medium for vocabulary acquisition, figurative language, narrative competence and oral proficiency. title: Developing multilingual literacy for Mozambican immigrant learners in Nsanje, Malawi: A braided river in the borderland multilingualism framework
text_snippet: Developing multilingual literacy for Mozambican immigrant learners in Nsanje, Malawi: A braided river in the borderland multilingualism framework Background: Border districts in southern Malawi experience recurrent cross-border displacement from Mozambique because of floods, cyclones and political instability. In Nsanje district, Mozambican immigrant learners enter schools with multilingual repertoires shaped by Sena and Portuguese, while Malawi’s 2014 language-in-education policy mandates a monolingual (English) medium of instruction from Standard 1. Objectives: The study examined how literacy for immigrant learners in Nsanje could be re-conceptualised to address the linguistic exclusion created by the monolingual language policy. It focused on a specific borderland context to explore the broader implications for multilingual literacy education in African settings affected by mobility. Method: The study employed a qualitative conceptual design. It analysed literature on literacy, language policy, multilingualism, border studies, and inclusive education. A theoretical synthesis was undertaken to examine the relationship between linguistic realities, literacy practices, and language-in-education policy. Results: The analysis indicated that monolingual policy assumptions undermine learners’ multilingual meaning-making practice

title: Refining preservice teachers’ vocabulary instruction through coaching and reflection using mixed reality simulations
text_snippet: Refining preservice teachers’ vocabulary instruction through coaching and reflection using mixed reality simulations Background: Effective vocabulary instruction underpins learners’ oral and reading comprehension; however, persistent comprehension difficulties in South African schools linked to limited vocabulary teaching highlight the need to strengthen preservice teachers’ instructional capacity. Objectives: This study examined how engagement in iterative cycles of practice, supported by coaching and reflection within mixed reality simulation (MRS) microlessons, enhances preservice teachers’ isiZulu vocabulary instruction in the Foundation Phase. Method: A qualitative interpretive case study design was used, drawing on lesson observations, coaching and reflection sessions, and focus group interviews. The study involved 19 second-year university students in Johannesburg preparing to teach isiZulu Home Language reading in Foundation Phase classrooms. Results: Preservice teachers initially struggled with appropriate word selection, systematic instruction, and the provision of learner-friendly definitions, resulting in fragmented explanations and limited learner understanding. title: Primary teacher education: A reflection on language in mathematics education
text_snippet: Primary teacher education: A reflection on language in mathematics education Background: South Africa is implementing a mother tongue-based bilingual education strategy. This shift in language policy has significant implications for mathematics teaching and for the preparation of mathematics teachers in initial teacher education (ITE) programmes. Objectives: The Primary Teacher Education (PrimTEd) knowledge and practice standards articulate the intended core curriculum for all primary teachers graduating from ITE programmes. This article examines the extent to which these standards are aligned with the emerging multilingual policy context. Method: We analysed the content of the PrimTEd Mathematics Knowledge and Practice Standards’, from a ‘language(s) in mathematics education’ perspective. All instances where language is explicitly referenced or implicitly invoked are identified and categorised. In critically reflecting on the findings, we note what is absent and illustrate how the policy framework could be strengthened. Results: Three approaches to language(s) are evident: through general pedagogical standards; through standards related to mathematical acting and thinking; and through the specification of knowledge of various problem types. title: Reflections on designing multiple-choice items for large-scale assessments of student teachers’ visual and critical visual literacy knowledge and practices
text_snippet: Reflections on designing multiple-choice items for large-scale assessments of student teachers’ visual and critical visual literacy knowledge and practices Background: The current Curriculum and Assessment Policy Statement (CAPS) for teaching languages and literacies in South African schools includes visual literacy components in all grades and thus teachers need to be visually literate, to be critical viewers of the visual, and to know how to teach visual and critical visual literacy. Objectives: The aim of this research was to investigate the possibilities of designing multiple-choice items that attempt to assess student teachers’ visual and critical visual literacy content and pedagogic knowledge. Method: In this reflective case study we present, discuss, and reflect on examples of multiple-choice items designed for the assessment of components of the Primary Teacher Education Project (PrimTEd). Our reflections are informed by literature in the fields of visual literacy and critical visual literacy education. Results: Sourcing socio-culturally inclusive, multimodal texts and creating appropriate classroom teaching scenarios on which to base questions that comply with the criterion of test fairness is challenging to achieve in any test format. title: From Jeddah to Jo’burg: Saudi boys’ reflections on issues of social justice in the novel Journey to Jo’burg
text_snippet: From Jeddah to Jo’burg: Saudi boys’ reflections on issues of social justice in the novel Journey to Jo’burg Background: Despite the growing recognition of the importance of diverse narratives, children’s literature sometimes lacks substantive representation of social justice themes, thereby limiting opportunities for critical engagement and awareness. The study seeks to investigate how exposure to such literature can cultivate critical thinking, empathy, and a heightened social consciousness among children. Through an analysis of their reflections, the research underscores the potential of literature as a transformative medium for fostering awareness and empowering young readers to recognise and question systemic inequalities. Objectives: The objective of the study was to explore how Grade 4 learners at a school in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, engage with and respond to social justice issues as presented in the novel Journey to Jo’burg Method: The study adopted a case study as a qualitative approach and, as a means of data generation, established a Reading Club as a type of focus group discussion. Results: The findings suggest that participants engaged with the social issues as presented in the story with empathetic understanding and thoughtful analysis. title: Finding voice through memoir writing: An exploration of the expression of grief in undergraduate students’ narratives
text_snippet: Finding voice through memoir writing: An exploration of the expression of grief in undergraduate students’ narratives Background: Memoir writing can be a powerful tool for authors to reflect on past events and express their emotions, especially those related to grief. Research suggests that, beyond narrating stories, memoir writing can fulfil a therapeutic purpose when based on personal experiences. Objectives: This article explores how first-year undergraduate students utilise memoir writing as a therapeutic means to express grief. In this article, memoir writing is employed not merely to recount events drawn from personal memories but also as a coping strategy that involves reflection upon traumatic experiences through written expression. It acts as a means for emotional expression and interrogation of thoughts. Method: Data were collected using qualitative approach aligned with a case study research design. The data collection process involved memoirs written by five first-year undergraduate students who participated in a Memoir Writing Project. In addition, thematic analysis was used to analyse the data. Results: The findings indicate that some students utilised the memoir writing process as a means of reflecting on their past traumatic experiences. In addition, the memoir writing process cont

title: Parents and caregivers in dyslexia research: A bibliometric review
text_snippet: Parents and caregivers in dyslexia research: A bibliometric review Background: Parents and caregivers play an important role in supporting children with dyslexia, particularly through home-based reading activities and informal learning support. Although parental involvement is widely acknowledged in dyslexia research, studies that explicitly examine parents’ challenges, expectations and roles in home-based support remain fragmented across disciplines. Objectives: This study aimed to map global publication trends, thematic emphases and intellectual structures in research on parents and caregivers in the context of dyslexia. Method: A bibliometric review was conducted using 437 peer-reviewed journal articles indexed in the Scopus database and published between 2000 and 2026. VOSviewer was used to examine international collaboration patterns, keyword co-occurrence networks and author co-citation structures. Results: The findings show that research output and collaboration are concentrated in high-income Western countries, particularly the United States and the United Kingdom, with limited representation from non-Western contexts. title: Agency and commitment in sustaining a university writing centre: A social realist perspective
text_snippet: Agency and commitment in sustaining a university writing centre: A social realist perspective Background: Massification of higher education has led to increased student diversity, and the growing realisation that academic discourse is a very specialised practice that students from all language backgrounds groups struggle to master. In addition, this article also examines the implications for writing centre practices and institutional level involvement, emphasising spaces where strategic mediation is needed. The inadequate writing skills of students is a result of the lack of guidance students often receive from lecturers. To address this problem, writing centres were established in universities and delegated to assist students to master academic writing. Objectives: The study aims to demonstrate how lecturers and students as primary agents apply their powers and properties to ensure the sustainability of the writing centre. Method: A qualitative method was employed in this study by conducting focus group interviews with 20 lecturers and 48 students from four different faculties through purposive sampling to evaluate their commitment to ensure the sustainability of the writing centre. title: The influence of Sepitori on Grade 6 learners’ Setswana writing in Winterveldt Tshwane: An essay writing analysis
text_snippet: The influence of Sepitori on Grade 6 learners’ Setswana writing in Winterveldt Tshwane: An essay writing analysis Background: In Winterveldt, a semi-rural community north of Pretoria, many children grow up speaking Sepitori, a non-standard urban variety, while being taught Setswana as their official home language in school. Objectives: This study investigates the influence of Sepitori on the Setswana literacy of Grade 6 learners in Winterveldt. Method: A qualitative, comparative design was employed, drawing on essay writing and semi-structured interviews as data collection methods. Participants included 100 learners selected randomly through purposive sampling, and three purposively sampled teachers from two schools. Results: Findings indicate that Sepitori significantly shapes learners’ written Setswana, often leading to language transfer in grammar, vocabulary, and spelling. Teachers expressed concern that learners are disadvantaged by being assessed in a language variety they seldom use outside the classroom, arguing that the disjuncture between Sepitori and standard Setswana undermines literacy development. Conclusion: The study concludes that non-standard varieties such as Sepitori should not be dismissed in educational contexts but rather acknowledged as resources that can support the ac

title: Reading comprehension in Sepedi foundation phase by Khelovedu learners
text_snippet: Reading comprehension in Sepedi foundation phase by Khelovedu learners Background: This study was prompted by the 2021 Progress in International Reading Literacy Study (PIRLS) results, which highlighted a serious reading crisis in South Africa, with Sepedi identified as the lowest-performing language in reading comprehension. Reading comprehension is vital because it provides the foundation for all subsequent learning, enabling learners to understand and engage meaningfully with content across all subjects. Objectives: This study examined learners’ reading comprehension in Sepedi during the Foundation Phase. Method: The study employed a qualitative case study design. Data were collected through classroom observations and semi-structured interviews with Grade 3 teachers from three selected primary schools in the Mopani District. Results: Learners’ comprehension of Sepedi texts in the Foundation Phase was generally poor. Learners experienced significant linguistic and phonological challenges, had limited vocabulary, and struggled to recall information and make inferences, indicating that many were unable to read for meaning. title: From compliance to agency: Leveraging mixed reality simulation to bridge the enactment gap in initial teacher education
text_snippet: From compliance to agency: Leveraging mixed reality simulation to bridge the enactment gap in initial teacher education Background: Although South Africa’s primary teacher education knowledge and practice standards establish clear literacy guidelines, an ‘enactment gap’ remains in initial teacher education (ITE). Components like oral reading fluency assessment and data-based instructional decision-making are often inadequately addressed, leaving pre-service teachers (PSTs) under-prepared to bridge theoretical knowledge and classroom application. Objectives: This study first audits the extent to which Foundation Phase Bachelor of Education (BEd) language modules represent these standards, moving beyond superficial mention to provide authentic practice-based approximations. Second, it investigates how an integrated module, featuring a practice-based learning cycle facilitated by mixed reality simulation (MRS), enables PSTs to move beyond procedural compliance toward data-based instructional decision-making. Method: Adopting a descriptive, instrumental case study design, this research unfolded in two phases. title: Informed by social justice? Fairness and inclusion in the Primary Teacher Education (PrimTEd) English language test item development
text_snippet: Informed by social justice? Fairness and inclusion in the Primary Teacher Education (PrimTEd) English language test item development Background: Historically, there has been an unevenness in South African language teaching at schools and in teacher education at universities, exacerbated by a lack of agreed course standards and gaps in what is offered in language courses on teacher education across universities. Objectives: This article argues that test design may contribute to greater equality – related to social justice – in education. Method: This article reports on aspects of test design that ensure fairness and give it relevance and cultural responsivity: the diversity of item writers; the development of culturally sensitive, realistic items based on language teaching and learning scenarios; the inclusion of a scaffolded free writing experience and varied question levels. Results: The authors describe how the test items bring notions of fairness to diversity of students and reflect the pedagogic realities of teaching English in a multilingual society. Conclusion: We argue that testing of the English language and literacies in initial teacher education has a social justice imperative, and that testing of these skills is necessary to interrupt a trajectory of teachers with limited language and pedagogic knowle

title: Students’ perspectives on writing an argumentative essay in an academic literacy module
text_snippet: Students’ perspectives on writing an argumentative essay in an academic literacy module Background: Argumentation, which is an important skill required of students in higher education, is often assessed through writing. It is a difficult skill for students to grasp, resulting in many challenges; however, it can be developed through practice and should receive greater attention, as it fosters the development of critical thinking skills, thereby better equips students to become active and democratic citizens. Objectives: This study reflects on first-year students’ perceptions and experiences of writing an argumentative essay in an Academic Literacy module. The aim of the study was to gain a better understanding of students’ writing challenges in order to develop meaningful ways of revising the course and ultimately enhancing their argumentative skills. Method: A qualitative approach was used, and data were collected by means of an online student questionnaire. The theoretical framework underpinning this research is socio-constructivism. title: Improving early grade reading for multilingual learners in English-medium classrooms: Evidence from the QondaRead programme in under-resourced schools in Makhanda, Eastern Cape
text_snippet: Improving early grade reading for multilingual learners in English-medium classrooms: Evidence from the QondaRead programme in under-resourced schools in Makhanda, Eastern Cape Background: South Africa’s early grade reading challenges are well documented and deeply systemic. Despite curriculum expectations that learners read with understanding by Grade 3, most, particularly in no-fee schools, fall short of this benchmark. The challenge is particularly acute for multilingual learners who speak an African language at home but attend English-medium schools. Objectives: Although policy supports mother tongue instruction to Grade 3, many learners enter straight-for-English classrooms with limited language support. Addressing this intersection of language, literacy, and inequality requires scalable, curriculum-aligned solutions. This study evaluates QondaRead, a low-cost, classroom-embedded literacy intervention piloted in four under-resourced English-medium schools in the Eastern Cape. Method: The programme integrates explicit phonics instruction, scaffolded fluency practice, and graded reader use into daily teaching. A mixed-method, pre–post design was employed with over 700 Grades 1–3 learners, complemented by teacher focus groups. title: Writing as developmental learning in L2 contexts: An interpretive case study using constructivist and register theory
text_snippet: Writing as developmental learning in L2 contexts: An interpretive case study using constructivist and register theory Background: Writing development in higher education requires both linguistic control and cognitive engagement. Register theory and constructivist pedagogy provide a framework for evaluating how students use language to persuade, reason, and reflect ethically in academic contexts. Objectives: To investigate how genre–based assessment and constructivist reflection in argumentative writing enhance developmental learning and rhetorical awareness among second–language university students. Method: Twenty–seven essays and 23 reflections were analysed. Essays were scored using register dimensions of field, tenor, and mode, while reflections were thematically coded for indicators of developmental learning. Results: Students wrote argumentative essays on artificial intelligence in education. Their control of tenor and mode was evident in persuasive organisation, while field scores reflected moderate lexical precision shaped by engagement with the theme. Reflections revealed metacognitive growth and ethical awareness, showing that students were both writing to learn and learning to write. title: Free voluntary reading approach for mitigating reading loss in rural English FAL Grade 10 classrooms
text_snippet: Free voluntary reading approach for mitigating reading loss in rural English FAL Grade 10 classrooms Background: Although the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic has significantly subsided, its educational repercussions persist, particularly in rural South African contexts. The abrupt transition to remote learning in 2020 disproportionately affected learners, particularly in under-resourced areas, resulting in significant learning loss – especially in reading among English First Additional Language (FAL) learners. Objectives: This qualitative study aimed to explore how the free voluntary reading (FVR) approach can be used to mitigate the COVID-19-induced reading loss among Grade 10 English FAL learners in a rural Free State school. Method: Grounded in Krashen’s Input Hypothesis Theory, the study adopted the Participatory Action Learning and Action Research methodology to engage two English FAL teachers and ten Grade 10 learners through purposive sampling. Data generated through semi-structured interviews, focus group discussions, and classroom observations were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Results: Findings reveal that the FVR approach significantly fostered improved reading confidence, motivation, comprehension, imagination, and vocabulary development. Con

title: Bridging the gap in teaching comprehension in English as First Additional Language in two Phases, Grade 3 and Grade 4 teachers’ perspective
text_snippet: Bridging the gap in teaching comprehension in English as First Additional Language in two Phases, Grade 3 and Grade 4 teachers’ perspective Background: Reading proficiency in English as a First Additional Language remains a critical challenge in South Africa and other countries. The 2021 Progress in International Reading Literacy Study starkly highlighted this issue, revealing that South African 10-year-olds perform at an extremely low level of reading for meaning, scoring 288 points far below the international centre point of 500 and ranking last among 65 participating education systems. Objectives: To investigate the pedagogical and systemic challenges teachers face in assisting learners with the transition from mother tongue instruction in the Foundation Phase to English as the primary language of teaching and learning at the start of Grade 4. Method: Informed by a constructivist paradigm, the research employed a qualitative approach. Twelve Grade 3 and Grade 4 language teachers were purposively sampled from four under-resourced rural schools. Data were collected through classroom observations and a semi-structured focus group interview to explore teaching practices. title: Code-switching in finance tutorials for immigrant students: An activity theory perspective
text_snippet: Code-switching in finance tutorials for immigrant students: An activity theory perspective Background: Given South Africa’s multilingual landscape and a growing immigrant student population, this study examines how code-switching enhances finance tutorials for African immigrant students at a South African university where English is the main medium of instruction. Objectives: The study focuses on an entrepreneurship programme, and examines how tutors switch between English and the tutee’s home or preferred languages to help students overcome language barriers and improve their understanding of complex financial concepts, such as the Time Value of Money. Method: Using a qualitative case study approach within an interpretivist paradigm, data were collected using focus group interviews and unobtrusive observations of tutorial sessions with five African immigrant tutees and three tutors. Two major themes emerged: the use of code-switching as a pedagogical tool and the role of tutors in meaning construction. Activity Theory served as the analytical frame for the study by enabling analysis of internal contradictions during tutorial activities. title: Teachers’ perspectives of the reading comprehension challenges and instructional strategies they use for Grade 8 EFAL learners
text_snippet: Teachers’ perspectives of the reading comprehension challenges and instructional strategies they use for Grade 8 EFAL learners Background: Reading comprehension instruction remains a cause of concern worldwide. Many studies have been conducted on the issue to provide possible strategies to assist readers with reading comprehension challenges. Objective: The study sought to investigate teachers’ perspectives on learners’ comprehension challenges and instructional strategies used for Grade 8 English First Additional Language (EFAL) learners. Method: This qualitative study employed a case study design and thematic data analysis to organise and analyse the data. The purposively selected sample for the semi-structured individual interviews comprised four Grade 8 EFAL teachers from four secondary schools chosen as a research site in the Capricorn North District, Koloti circuit. Results: Teachers believed that learners experience challenges because of overcrowding, limited vocabulary, and pronunciation. Most importantly, learners’ native language makes it a challenge because they speak Sepedi in class. The results further indicate that all four teachers concurred in their responses about the reading strategies and engagement strategies they used. More disturbingly, teachers relied on traditional teaching methods.

title: Community engagement: Resourced reading clubs in 12 rural primary schools in the Eastern Cape
text_snippet: Community engagement: Resourced reading clubs in 12 rural primary schools in the Eastern Cape Background: Low literacy levels in South African rural primary schools continue to be challenging, with many schools not having access to adequate resources. The private higher education institution (HEI) responded to a call for authentic, meaningful engagement to become an implementing partner in a rural district for literacy development intervention, which was funded by an education support foundation. Objectives: The study focused on examining the perceptions and responses of teachers and reading club facilitators to resourced reading clubs as a vehicle for literacy development in 12 rural primary schools in the Eastern Cape. Method: Employing a qualitative, multi-site case study positioned within a constructivist paradigm explored how through community engagement-resourced reading clubs were used as a vehicle for literacy development in 12 rural primary schools; data were gathered through observation, monthly facilitator feedback reports, open-ended questionnaires, and focus group discussions with teachers, reading club facilitators, and monitors. title: Exploring the relationship between syntactic complexity, error types, and pedagogical implications in advanced writing: A quantitative analysis
text_snippet: Exploring the relationship between syntactic complexity, error types, and pedagogical implications in advanced writing: A quantitative analysis Background: This study investigates the relationship where common linguistic errors may act as constraints on the attainment of syntactic complexity and explores the resulting pedagogical implications in advanced writing. Objective: The exploration of error patterns has been conducted to analyse sentence structure and instructional strategies in the advanced writing teaching process. The main objective of the research is to find a connection between the common linguistic errors that might serve as barriers to syntactic complexity being achieved, and a discussion of consequent pedagogical implications in advanced writing. Method: The investigation employs a quantitative approach in which the essays of 100 undergraduate students are analysed, and the relationship between the different features of syntactic complexity is examined. The features of syntactic complexity in the research studied include the mean number of words before the verb (SYNLE), the average number of modifiers per noun phrase (SYNNP), and sentence-to-sentence similarity. title: Perspectives on oral reading fluency, vocabulary and reading comprehension in bilingual learners from Ghana, South Africa and Zimbabwe
text_snippet: Perspectives on oral reading fluency, vocabulary and reading comprehension in bilingual learners from Ghana, South Africa and Zimbabwe Background: While oral reading fluency (ORF) is linked to reading comprehension (RC) in African languages, the role of vocabulary remains underexplored. Objectives: This study investigated the relative contributions of ORF and vocabulary to RC in the first and second languages of three bilingual groups: Akan-English in Ghana, isiZulu-English in South Africa, and Shona-English in Zimbabwe and examined the ORF rate needed for 80% comprehension in each language. Method: A quantitative correlational design was used. Learners in Ghana (n = 158), South Africa (n =104), and Zimbabwe (n = 122) were assessed through convenience sampling. Constructs measured included: ORF, RC and receptive vocabulary tests. Results: Oral reading fluency was a strong predictor of RC in first and second languages. Learners needed to read between 89 and 109 words correct per minute (WCPM) in English to achieve 80% comprehension. For African languages ORF thresholds ranged from 47 WCPM (isiZulu) to 55 WCPM (Akan). Conclusion: Oral reading fluency emerged as a critical prerequisite for RC across bilingual populations. title: Source integration practices and pedagogical implications in English academic writing: A case study of Omani undergraduates
text_snippet: Source integration practices and pedagogical implications in English academic writing: A case study of Omani undergraduates Background: College students often struggle with integrating sources because of unclear academic expectations and limited instruction. This study examines these challenges to inform the development of more effective pedagogical support. Objectives: The purpose of this research is to analyse the challenges faced by English as a Foreign Language students in applying APA-style citation and referencing, as well as in summarising and paraphrasing. Using assessment data drawn from the institutional course learning outcomes (CLOs) dashboard, the study evaluates the extent to which these academic writing skills have been mastered and, in turn, determines the efficacy of current teaching strategies. Methods: Data from 60 ENG101 students at the Modern College of Business and Science in Muscat, Oman, were analysed quantitatively using a standardised assessment rubic to assess source-integration skills. Institutional CLOs’ dashboard figures were also reviewed to validate rubric scores, and to identify citation and paraphrasing trends. title: Examining how undergraduate students view reading and its significance
text_snippet: Examining how undergraduate students view reading and its significance Background: Low literacy levels have been demonstrated by several university students, which has impacted their academic achievement. To solve this issue, prior research indicates that a positive attitude typically translates into better academic performance, whereas a negative attitude towards reading will have the opposite effect. Research shows that low reading proficiency from school, a lack of intrinsic motivation, restricted access to reading resources, and a lack of a reading culture at home are the root causes of South African university students’ negative attitudes towards reading. Objectives: Thus, the goal of the current study was to determine how students felt about reading and its importance in their academic lives. Method: The study used a case study design and was qualitative in nature. Twenty-four students who were conveniently chosen were given an open-ended questionnaire. The data were analysed using content analysis. Results: Depending on whether the reading material was relevant to their interests, students’ responses varied. title: Educators of inmates: Reflections on a five-day Reading-for-Meaning workshop
text_snippet: Educators of inmates: Reflections on a five-day Reading-for-Meaning workshop Background: The Department of Correctional Services recognises the urgent need to improve access to rehabilitation programmes, to prepare for successful reintegration into society. Despite many correctional services policy documents stating that every child has a right to education, professional development courses have not been offered to educators of inmates. Objectives: Using Vygotsky’s and Bandura’s theories we explored the learning experiences of educators of inmates using innovative Reading-for-Meaning literacy pedagogical practices. Our objective was for the educators to challenge the inmates’ world views about solving problems, thereby attempting to reduce the recidivism rates in South Africa. Method: This study used an interpretive paradigm, a qualitative approach, and a case study design. Pre- and post-questionnaires were used to collect data from 58 educators of prisoners, of whom 44 educators completed the post-questionnaire. title: Teachers’ perceptions about the implementation of Early Grade Reading Assessment
text_snippet: Teachers’ perceptions about the implementation of Early Grade Reading Assessment Background: Reading proficiency of learners remains problematic. In South Africa, teaching reading has often proven ineffective. The lack of proficient reading skills has been one of the leading catalysts for implementing reading intervention campaigns, such as the Early Grade Reading Studies (EGRS). The Early Grade Reading Assessment (EGRA) tool was developed to enable teachers to gain insight into learners’ reading abilities and to make informed instructional decisions regarding their reading instruction. Since the implementation of the EGRA tool country-wide, teachers’ perceptions regarding this assessment tool have not received any attention. The possible influence that teachers’ perceptions of the EGRA can have on the effective implementation thereof underpinned the rationale of this study. Objectives: Foundation Phase teachers’ perceptions of the EGRA were explored to gain an in-depth understanding of teachers’ intentions to use EGRA to inform their reading instruction. Method: The study uses a quantitative survey research design to explore teachers’ perceptions of EGRA as an influential variable. title: Words matter – but how? A study of high school learners’ vocabulary and reading comprehension
text_snippet: Words matter – but how? A study of high school learners’ vocabulary and reading comprehension Background: Learners’ vocabulary knowledge in English additional language (EAL) can serve as an indicator of their reading comprehension as well as their chances of academic success. Objectives: This article describes and examines patterns and relationships between the vocabulary knowledge of Grade 11 learners at different word frequency levels (2000, 3000, 5000, university word list and 10 000 word level) and their reading comprehension performance. Method: In this cross-sectional study quantitative data were collected from 67 senior high school EAL learners in two low-performing schools from a low socio-economic context in the Zambezi region in Namibia. A vocabulary levels test and a reading comprehension test were used to assess the EAL learners. Results: The results showed that the learners had limited vocabulary knowledge and low comprehension levels. The study found a significant modest correlation between knowledge of vocabulary and reading comprehension. The study further revealed that while all word levels correlated significantly with reading comprehension, the 5000 word level emerged as the strongest predicator of reading comprehension. title: Using a wordless picture book to explore children’s narrative production in rural Kenya
text_snippet: Using a wordless picture book to explore children’s narrative production in rural Kenya Background: Early language development is critical for literacy acquisition and academic success. However, children in rural Africa often face challenges such as limited access to literacy resources and minimal shared reading experiences at home, which can hinder their language skills. While wordless picture books (WPBs) are known to enhance narrative abilities, scant research has examined their effectiveness in rural African contexts. Objectives: This study explored how WPBs support narrative development among preschool children in rural Kenya. It examined the relationship between home literacy environments, parental involvement, and children’s storytelling abilities. Method: A mixed-methods approach was used, combining qualitative thematic analysis of children’s storytelling with quantitative data on family reading practices. Forty preschool children participated in WPB-based storytelling sessions, while parents completed structured interviews on home literacy practices. Data were analysed thematically and statistically to identify patterns in children’s narrative responses. title: Exploring postgraduate students’ understanding and integration of a theoretical framework
text_snippet: Exploring postgraduate students’ understanding and integration of a theoretical framework Background: The integration of a theoretical framework is a fundamental component of postgraduate research, as it provides conceptual grounding, guides data analysis, and strengthens scholarly argumentation. However, many postgraduate students struggle to understand, select, and meaningfully integrate theoretical frameworks into their research projects. Objectives: This study explored postgraduate students’ understanding of theoretical frameworks and examined how they integrate them into their research. Method: The study employed a qualitative case study research design. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews from postgradaute (masters and doctoral) students at a South African university. The data were analysed thematically to identify recurring patterns related to students’ conceptual understanding and application of theory. Results: The study found that many postgraduate students have a limited and fragmented understanding of theoretical frameworks.
